claims.text: Introducing chemically distinct barrier layers into an HEA coating reduces time-dependent plastic deformation relative to a monolithic HEA coating.
Nanolayered HEA/graphene coatings can be fabricated using controlled deposition and transfer processes.
The proposed controlled comparison is between a monolithic HEA coating and an otherwise identically processed HEA/barrier multilayer.
Time-dependent creep is measurable under constant applied stress at room and elevated temperatures in the proposed coatings.
The HEA and barrier layers form coherent interfaces.
Chemically distinct HEA/graphene interfaces are present in nanolayered CoCrFeNi/graphene composites.
Interfacial barrier layers hinder dislocation propagation.
Interfacial barrier layers reduce the rate of lattice diffusion.
Lattice diffusion of constituent elements can govern creep deformation.
Obstacles to dislocation motion require additional force for dislocations to overcome them.
Reduced lattice diffusion and obstructed dislocation motion increase the energy barrier for dislocation climb and movement.
The proposed interfacial mechanism produces significantly lower creep strain over time than occurs in monolithic HEA coatings.
The creep-resistance mechanism is effective only when the barrier layers are coherent and chemically distinct.
Degraded interface quality diminishes the creep-resistance effect.
Nonoptimal layer thickness diminishes the creep-resistance effect.
The magnitude of creep reduction and its sensitivity to interface spacing and barrier material have not been quantitatively determined.
Failure to observe both a statistically significant creep-strain reduction and impeded dislocation motion in the multilayer relative to the monolithic control would falsify the hypothesis.
